sections.eli10:
### Question 1

Think of a medical word like a sandwich. The word root is the meat in the middle, the main thing the sandwich is really about. The bread and toppings (prefixes and suffixes) just change how it tastes, but the meat tells you what you're eating. So cardi- means the word is about the heart, no matter what gets added around it.

### Question 2

In a medical word, the ending is like the last word of a sentence that tells you what happened. If a word ends in -itis, something is swollen and sore. The ending always waits at the back of the word, like the caboose at the end of a train.

### Question 3

The little 'o' is like oil that helps two puzzle pieces snap together smoothly. Cardi + megaly would be hard to say, so we slip in an 'o' to get cardiomegaly. The 'o' doesn't mean anything by itself; it just makes the word roll off your tongue.

### Question 4

The combining vowel is a helper that only shows up when the word would be hard to say. If the ending already starts with a vowel sound, you don't need the helper, so it steps aside. Gastritis flows nicely; gastroitis would trip your tongue.

### Question 5

Read the word in pieces like train cars. Peri- rides up front and means 'around.' Cardi- is the middle and means 'heart.' -itis is the caboose and means 'swollen and sore.' Put them together: something around the heart is inflamed.

### Question 6

A prefix is the hello at the start of the word, often telling you where or when or how many. A suffix is the goodbye at the end, often telling you what is happening, like a problem or a surgery. Front says where; back says what. The middle root names the body part, and the little vowel that glues pieces together belongs to that root.

### Question 7

The ending is the verb of the word. -tomy means 'make a cut,' but -ectomy means 'take it out.' Keep the stomach part the same and just swap the ending, and you go from opening the stomach to removing it.

### Question 8

Break it up: hepat means liver and -megaly means 'big.' So hepatomegaly is a big liver. The word literally tells you the size problem if you read the ending, just like 'mega' means huge in everyday words.

### Question 9

Some words have two body-part pieces plus an ending. Here electr means electricity, cardi means heart, and -gram means the picture or printout. So it's the printout of the heart's electricity. The -gram ending is the paper you can hold, not the machine or the act of making it.

### Question 10

Look at the tail of the word first. -scopy means 'taking a look inside with a special camera-tube.' Once you know a look-inside is happening, you just add where: the colon. The ending gives the action; the front gives the place. Note that -scope would be the tube itself, while -scopy is the act of using it.

### Question 11

This word had two body parts glued together: bone (oste) and joint (arthr). Take the joint piece out and you're left with just bone plus 'inflamed.' The word now points only at bone, because every body-part piece you remove takes its meaning with it.

### Question 12

Same kidney root, three different endings, three different jobs. -logy is 'studying it,' -pathy is 'something's wrong with it,' and -ectomy is 'taking it out.' The ending is the boss of the word: keep the kidney the same and the ending decides the whole story.
